newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa set to count blacks for first time.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa set to count blacks for first time.

text.p: South Africa will count all its black residents for the first time in a national census starting on Thursday, ending the apartheid practice of estimating their numbers from aerial photographs of townships.
The three-week census, under the slogan "Count Us In", will be the first conducted since all-race elections in 1994 hammered the final nail into apartheid's coffin.

Until as recently as 1991, when the last census was held, South Africa was not even counted as a single nation -- blacks living in the four nominally independent homelands and several other self-governing states were counted separately from the rest of "white" South Africa.
The census also aims to ascertain how many illegal immigrants are in the country -- estimates range from two million to eight million or higher.

In an innovative bid to count the country's untold thousands of homeless people, the government Central Statistical Service (CSS) has invited them to 120 street parties to be held across the land on Wednesday night.

"We've spent months talking to homeless children and adults, gaining their trust and trying convince them to go to the parties, because they've never been counted before," CSS spokeswoman Theresa Pretorius told Reuters.

Deputy director of the census Hennie Loots said it was essential not only to arrive at a population count, but to obtain details of everyone in the country, whether or not he or she was legally resident.
"A true census is by definition the survey which includes the details of each and every individual of a population," Loots said.
More than 80,000 enumerators visiting an estimated one million households will carry questionnaires in all 11 official languages.

Loots said the 356 million rand ($78.5 million) exercise would provide accurate information on unemployment to the government and private sector and would identify areas with urgent needs for water, electricity, schools, hospitals or roads.
In its search to provide the statistical platform from which the country's social and economic liberation can be launched, Census '96 provides temporary jobs for at least 102,000 people.
A University of South Africa (Unisa) market-research survey published in August showed the black population had increased by 713,200 between 1995 and 1996, 21 times more than the white population.
From 1991 the number of blacks increased by 2.4 percent from more than 28 million to 32 million, it said.
In comparison, the white population increased by less than one percent from 5.1 to 5.2 million.
In the two other main population groups, Asians have added 13,500 to their numbers per year, while there are 48,600 more Coloureds (people of mixed-race decent) than last year.

The university estimates the country's population, excluding illegal aliens, now totals 41.8 million, representing a growth of 810,000 (2.1 percent) for all population groups for one year since 1995. ($1=4.53 rand)
